This study investigates levels of cuproptosis markers in Wilson disease (WD) and their role in the occurrence and development of WD. We retrospectively collected clinical data from 76 patients with Leipzig score ≥ 4 hospitalized in the First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui University of Chinese Medicine from January 2023 to September 2023. The participants were given copper chelators (sodium dimercaptosulphonate (20 mg·kg −1 ), 4 courses of treatment, 32 days). The levels of clinical indicators (ALT, AST, ALP, HA, LN, PIIINP, CIV, liver stiffness measurement, United Wilson disease rating scale), oxidative stress indexes (SOD, MDA, GSH), cuproptosis markers (FDX1, DLAT, LIAS, ACO-2, SDHB, PLOD1, DPYD) of the participants were measured before and after treatment. Compared with the control group, FDX1, DLAT, DPYD, and POLD1 in WD were significantly up-regulated before treatment (6464.34 ± 2980.66 vs 4125.43 ± 2230.13 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 1364.36 ± 376.81 vs 884.22 ± 175.42 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 279.74 ± 123.63 vs 155.68 ± 67.32 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 3536.11 ± 1404.83 vs 1487.76 ± 658.26 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001), while SDHB was significantly down-regulated (2458.75 ± 1103.75 vs 5338.22 ± 921.54 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .05). SOD was significantly down-regulated before treatment (13.20 ± 2.06 vs 13.27 ± 1.79 U ⋅ mgprot −1 , P < .05), while MDA and GSH were significantly up-regulated (10.53 ± 4.76 vs 4.92 ± 1.81 nmol ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 49.28 ± 25.55 vs 24.70 ± 12.01 µol ⋅ L −1 , P < .001). POLD1 were down-regulated (3536.11 ± 1404.83 vs 1487.76 ± 658.26 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001), and SDHB was up-regulated after treatment (2458.75 ± 1103.75 vs2709.61 ± 906.95 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .05), while SOD, MDA and GSH were significantly down-regulated (13.20 ± 2.06 vs 12.48 ± 1.52 U ⋅ mgprot −1 , P < .05, 10.53 ± 4.76 vs 7.65 ± 3.65 nmol ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 49.28 ± 25.55 vs 34.09 ± 15.02 µmol ⋅ L −1 , P < .001). The expression levels of cuproptosis markers and oxidative stress indexes are abnormal in WD patients. Introduction Hepatolenticular degeneration, also known as the Wilson disease (WD), is induced by ATP7B gene mutation, which causes partial or complete loss of function of the copper-transporting P-type ATPase. As a result, excess Cu 2+ cannot be transported out of the cell, resulting in excessive Cu 2+ deposition in the liver, brain, kidney, cornea, and other tissues, thus causing diseases. WD causes brain degeneration and is mainly characterized by liver cirrhosis and basal ganglia damage. The clinical manifestations of WD mainly include progressively worsening extrapyramidal symptoms, psychiatric symptoms, cirrhosis of the liver, renal impairment, and corneal pigment rings. [ 1 ] Copper is one of the essential trace elements in the human body. Free Cu 2+ is a cofactor or key component of more than 30 enzymes and copper-containing proteins in the body, which plays an important role in many physiological processes, such as mitochondria metabolism and the maintenance of oxidation-reduction homeostasis. [ 2 ] Studies have demonstrated that Cu 2+ destabilizes the accumulation of lipoacylated proteins and iron-sulfur cluster protein by directly binding to lipoacylated parts in the tricarboxylic acid cycle, leading to protein toxicity stress, thus inducing apoptosis-independent cell death. Furthermore, excessive Cu 2+ can lead to abnormal cell function and promote the generation of reactive oxygen species, inducing Haber - Weiss reaction and subsequent Fenton reaction, leading to copper-related cuproptosis and iron-related ferroptosis. [ 3 , 4 ] Tsvetkov et al explored liver pathology in Atp7b-homozygous (Atp7b−/−), Atp7b heterozygous (Atp7b−/+), and wild-type mice and found that copper overload results in the same cellular effects as cuproptosis, characterized by accumulation of lipoacylated proteins and iron-sulfur cluster protein instability. [ 5 ] Xu et al suggested that the absence of iron-sulfur proteins and lipoacylated proteins induces mitochondria damage, further inducing cell death. [ 6 ] However, the role of Cu 2+ carriers in cell death in WD disease progression and diagnosis is unknown. This study aimed to investigate the expression levels of cuproptosis markers in WD and explore their roles in the occurrence and development of WD. Therefore, this study may provide references for clinical diagnosis and treatment of WD.

2. Materials and methods 2.1. Clinical observation 2.1.1. General information A total of 76 WD patients’s clinical data in the First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui University of Chinese Medicine from January 2023 to September 2023 were respectively collected in this study (Fig. 1 ). The patients were aged 5 to 57 years (average; 26.02 ± 10.58 years), and their disease courses ranged from 0.01 to 33 years (average;9.32 ± 7.24 years) (Table 1 ). 2.1.2. Diagnostic criteria The diagnostic criteria that Leipzig score ≥ 4 were developed based on the 2021 edition of “Chinese Hepatolenticular Degeneration Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines 2021” by the Neurogenetics Group of the Neurology Branch of the Chinese Medical Association [ 7 ] and the 2022 edition of the “Hepatolenticular Degeneration Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines 2022” by the Genetic Metabolic Liver Diseases Collaborative Group of the Hepatology Branch of the Chinese Medical Association. [ 8 ] 2.1.3. Inclusion criteria Inclusion criteria included: individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria of WD and individuals who did not receive formal copper discharge treatment before admission. This study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui University of Chinese Medicine (No. 2023AH-03). Notably, the patients or their family members signed a written informed consent before participating. 2.1.4. Exclusion criteria Exclusion criteria included: individuals who were previously diagnosed and treated with formal copper discharge therapy; patients with fulminant hepatic failure (with or without hemolytic anemia) and decompensated liver cirrhosis; patients with comorbid cognitive dysfunction (mini-mental state examination score ≤ 22 or Montreal cognitive assessment score < 26); patients with severe neurological impairment, such as torsion spasms; individuals with comorbid psychiatric illness; individuals with moderate, severe or total dependence in daily life (Barthel index score ≤ 70); individuals with severe comorbidities (opportunistic infections, tumors, and hematological disorders); pregnant and lactating women. 2.1.5. Treatment The patients were given a low-copper diet. Conventional chelation therapy was given using sodium dimercaptosulphonate (DMPS) (2 mL: 0.125 g, Shanghai Hefeng Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.). Specifically, DMPS (20 mg·kg −1 ) was intravenously given by dissolving it in 5% glucose or 0.9% sodium chloride solution once a day for 6 days. Calcium gluconate (20 mL) injection, dissolved in 5% glucose, was administered intravenously during the intervals once a day for 2 days. Four courses of treatment were conducted, where 8 days were considered as 1 course of treatment. 2.1.6. Indicator analysis Fasting peripheral venous blood (5 mL) was collected before and after treatment, then the serum was centrifuged using an H1850 medical centrifuge (Hunan Xiangyi Laboratory Instrument Development Co., Ltd.). 2.1.6.1. Clinical indicators Clinical indicators included; liver injury indexes [alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP)); hepatic fibrosis indexes (hyaluronic acid (HA), laminin (LN), N-terminal peptide of type III procollagen (PIIINP), type IV collagen (CIV), liver stiffness measurement (LSM)]; United WD rating scale (UWDRS). 2.1.6.2. Copper -related indicators We measured serum copper, ceruloplasmin, copper in 24-h urinary excretion, and further to calculate non-ceruloplasmin-bound copper (NCBC) based on “EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: WD” by European Association for the Study of the Liver, as follows: NCBC = serum (mg/L) – ceruloplasmin (g/L) × 3.15. [ 9 ] 2.1.6.3. Oxidative stress indexes The serum levels of superoxide dismutase (SOD), malondialdehyde (MDA), and glutathione (GSH) were determined via the xanthine oxidase method, thiobarbituric acid method, and dithiodinitrobenzoic acid method, respectively. The absorbance was determined according to the corresponding wavelengths, and the content was calculated using the formula. 2.1.6.4. Cuproptosis markers ELISA was used to detect the levels of ferredoxin1 (FDX1), human dihydrolipoamide S-acetyltransferase (DLAT), human lipoic acid synthetase (LIAS), human Aconitase 2 (ACO-2), human succinate dehydrogenase complex iron-sulfur subunit B (SDHB), human DNA polymerase delta 1, catalytic subunit (PLOD1), and human dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPYD). 2.1.6.5. Safety indexes Blood routine, urine routine, stool routine, liver function, renal function, and electrocardiogram were conducted before and after treatment. Also, adverse reactions, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and skin rash were observed. 2.1.7. Statistical analysis SPSS 26.0 was used for all data analysis. Normally distributed data were expressed as mean and standard deviation ( χ ¯ ± s ) by t -test (paired t -test for intragroup comparison before and after treatment, and group t -test for inter-group comparison) and Pearson correlation analysis. Data that did not meet normal distribution were expressed as the median and quartile intervals [ M ( P 25 , P 75 )] by Wilcoxon rank sum test and Spearman correlation analysis. P < .05 was considered a statistically significant difference. 3. Results 3.1. Clinical indicators PIIINP, CIV, and LSM were significantly down-regulated after treatment (38.80 ± 21.69 vs 24.12 ± 14.51 ng ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 86.75 ± 55.48 vs 69.08 ± 25.73 ng ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 10.92 ± 4.74 vs 9.01 ± 4.68 kPa, P < .05), while the levels of ALT, AST, ALP, HA, LN, and UWDRS were not significant differences ( P > .05, Table 2 and Fig. 2 ). 3.2. Copper-related indicators Levels of serum copper, copper in 24-h urinary excretion and NCBC has significantly decreased after treatment. (0.26 ± 0.16 vs 0.19 ± 0.11 µmol ⋅ L −1 , P < .05, 1112.41 ± 686.42 vs 717.87 ± 318.65 µg ⋅ 24 h −1 , P < .05, 0.14 ± 0.15 vs 0.09 ± 0.11 mg ⋅ L −1 , P < .05, Table 3 and Fig. 3 ). 3.3. Oxidative stress indexes Compared with the control group, SOD was down-regulated before treatment (13.20 ± 2.06 vs 13.27 ± 1.79 U ⋅ mgprot −1 , P < .05), while MDA and GSH were up-regulated (10.53 ± 4.76 vs 4.92 ± 1.81 µmol ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 49.28 ± 25.55 vs 24.70 ± 12.01 µmol ⋅ L −1 , P < .001). SOD, MDA, and GSH were significantly down-regulated after treatment (13.20 ± 2.06 vs 12.48 ± 1.52 U ⋅ mgprot −1 , P < .05, 10.53 ± 4.76 vs 7.65 ± 3.65 µmol ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 49.28 ± 25.55 vs 34.09 ± 15.02 µmol ⋅ L −1 , P < .001), Notably, MDA remained up-regulated, SOD and GSH levels were not significantly different after treatment ( P < .05, Table 4 and Fig. 4 4). 3.4. Cuproptosis markers Compared with the control group, DLAT, DPYD, FDX1, and POLD1 were significantly up-regulated before treatment (6464.34 ± 2980.66 vs 4125.43 ± 2230.13 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 1364.36 ± 376.81 vs 884.22 ± 175.42 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 279.74 ± 123.63 vs 155.68 ± 67.32 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 3536.11 ± 1404.83 vs 1487.76 ± 658.26 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001), while SDHB was significantly down-regulated (2458.75 ± 1103.75 vs 5338.22 ± 921.54 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .05). SDHB was significantly up-regulated after treatment, while POLD1 was down-regulated (2458.75 ± 1103.75 vs2709.61 ± 906.95 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .05, 3536.11 ± 1404.83 vs 1487.76 ± 658.26 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001). Notably, FDX1 levels did not significantly change after treatment ( P > .05, see Table 5 and Fig. 5 ). 3.5. Correlation analysis of hepatic fibrosis indexes and cuproptosis markers Correlation analysis revealed that HA had an extremely weak correlation with DLAT ( R = 0.1817, P = .0363), PIIINP had an extremely weak correlation with MDA (| r| = 0.1733, P = .0461), PIIINP had a weak correlation with DLAT (| r| = 0.2048, P = .0181), and CIV had weak correlations with MDA (| r| = 0.2182, P = .0116) and SDHB ( R = 0.2846, P = .0009, Fig. 6 ). 3.6. Correlation analysis of clinical indicators and cuproptosis markers UWDRS had a weak correlation with FDX1 ( R = 0.2393, P = .0126) and extremely weak correlations with LIAS ( R = 0.1939, P = .0443) and SDHB (| r| = 0.1927, P = .0457, see Fig. 6 ). 3.7. Safety indexes Blood routine examination, urine routine examination, stool routine examination, liver function test, renal function test, and electrocardiogram showed no significant abnormalities during the treatment period. However, 3 patients experienced drug-related adverse reactions, including rashes, fever, and itchy rash around the eyelids and mouth, which were relieved after symptomatic treatment. 4. Discussion Ferredoxin 1 (FDX1) is a key upstream regulator of the cuproptosis pathway. FDX1 can reduce Cu 2+ to more toxic Cu + that induce the aggregation of lipoacylated dihydrolipoamide S-acetyltransferase (DLAT, LIAS), and subsequently promote iron-sulfur cluster protein loss (SDHB, ACO-2, PLOD, DPYD), leading to liver injury in WD with cuproptosis related to copper and ferroptosis to iron. [ 4 , 10 ] In this study, WD had high Cu 2+ levels, and the abnormally elevated FDX1 reduced Cu 2+ to Cu + , catalyzing the lipoacylation of DLAT, DLST, and LIAS. Moreover, the Cu + is further bound to the lipoacylated sites of DLAT, resulting in significant oligomerization of DLAT and leading to copper toxicity. Iron-sulfur clusters are inorganic cofactors in the human body, which can be embedded into the apoprotein to form multiple iron-sulfur proteins, of which a variety of key enzymes are involved in electron transfer, energy metabolism, gene expression regulation, and other important physiological processes. The structural and functional abnormalities and synthesis disorders of iron-sulfur proteins can cause metabolic or functional disorders and even lead to death. [ 11 , 12 ] Copper metabolism is closely related to iron-sulfur proteins and can affect the growth and maturation of iron-sulfur proteins in the mitochondria. [ 13 ] This may lead to the abnormal expression and dysfunction of iron-sulfur proteins in a feedback manner. [ 14 ] Li et al constructed a high-copper cell model and found that the high-copper state can inhibit iron-sulfur cluster assembly and function. This can also affect the respiratory chain complex active agent mitochondria metabolism, resulting in the change of the mitochondria morphology. [ 15 ] However, the level of ACO-2 did not show any significant abnormality, consistent with previous studies. [ 16 ] In this study, WD had a disorder of iron-sulfur proteins, resulting in significant up-regulation of DPYD and POLD1 and down-regulation of SDHB. [ 17 ] Oligomerization of DLAT and disorder of iron-sulfur proteins affect energy metabolism. Studies have demonstrated that [ 18 ] cell apoptosis rate increases with increasing Cu 2+ concentration, especially after 5 to 20 μmol/L Cu 2+ exposure ( P < .01). Specifically, ≥5 μmol/L Cu 2+ significantly increases intracellular reactive oxygen species and MDA levels ( P < .05), while significantly decreasing GSH and SOD activities ( P < .05). However, only 20 μmol/L Cu 2+ exposure can significantly decrease catalase activity ( P < .05). Copper overload can damage mitochondria in the brain, liver, and other tissues, as evidenced by a structural abnormality of mitochondria and abnormal expression of microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 in mitochondria. [ 19 , 20 ] In this study, SOD was down-regulated before treatment, while MDA and GSH were up-regulated compared with the control group, suggesting that WD patients showed enhanced oxidative stress responses in vivo and significant oxidative damage. Cupropotosis is distinct from known regulatory cell death mechanisms, characterized by the accumulation of lipoacylated proteins and iron-sulfur cluster protein instability. Studies have shown that cellular effects induced by copper overload in WD are similar to those induced by Cu 2+ . [ 4 , 5 ] This pathway is dependent on the accumulation of Cu 2+ in cells, and chelation therapy are preferred in the treatment of this disease. However, it is unclear whether copper chelating agents induce the cell death pathway or whether Cu 2+ redeposition after the use of chelation therapy induces cuproptosis. In this study, POLD1 was down-regulated after treatment, while SDHB, DLAT, DPYD, LIAS, and POLD1 remained up-regulated compared with the control group. Furthermore, GSH, MDA, and SOD were significantly down-regulated after treatment ( P < .05), indicating that copper chelating agents can effect on cuproptosis, thereby relieving the disorder of iron-sulfur cluster protein and damages caused by oxidative stress. Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) is the smallest complex in the respiratory chain of the mitochondria intima, and it is responsible for catalyzing the oxidation of succinic acid in the tricarboxylic acid cycle. [ 21 ] SDH consists of A, B, C, and D subunits. SDHB is a hydrophilic iron-sulfur protein that promotes the oxidation of succinic acid to participate in substance metabolism. [ 22 ] Herein, SDHB was down-regulated before treatment compared with the control group, affecting succinic acid metabolism, thus leading to a large accumulation of succinic acid in mitochondria, affecting the mitochondria energy metabolism pathway. However, SDHB was up-regulated after treatment, enhancing the restoration o

tes the oxidation of succinic acid to participate in substance metabolism. [ 22 ] Herein, SDHB was down-regulated before treatment compared with the control group, affecting succinic acid metabolism, thus leading to a large accumulation of succinic acid in mitochondria, affecting the mitochondria energy metabolism pathway. However, SDHB was up-regulated after treatment, enhancing the restoration of the mitochondria metabolic pathway to normal.Nonetheless, the expression level of SDHB is inconsistent with other cupropotosis markers that requires further study. The liver is one of the most WD-affected organs. Liver damage present in varying degrees at the time of WD diagnosis, which can be manifested clinically as asymptomatic, acute hepatitis, acute liver failure, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and other forms. [ 23 – 25 ] Liver damage can gradually progress to hepatic fibrosis as the disease progresses, eventually leading to cirrhosis, associated with various clinical manifestations, such as upper gastrointestinal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, infection, and portal vein thrombosis or spongiform degeneration. [ 26 ] Hepatic fibrosis promotes the development of liver damage into cirrhosis in WD. However, effective interventions against hepatic fibrosis can delay or even reverse the progression of liver damage to cirrhosis to improve the clinical prognosis of the patients. [ 27 , 28 ] In this study, hepatic fibrosis indexes (PIIINP, CIV, and LSM) were decreased. These indexes had significant correlations with cuproptosis markers and clinical indicators, suggesting that cuproptosis pathway might be involved in preventing WD hepatic fibrosis progression. However, this study has some limitations. First, only the levels of key proteins of copper death were measured, necessitating further screening and validation for the specific differentially expressed proteins of WD-copper death. Second, although we have tried to collect clinical data from patients as comprehensively as possible, some data were incomplete due to as retrospective study, and may influence the observational indexes. Third, the patients were treated with sodium dimercaptopropane sulfonate for copper discharge, and further research is needed to report the effects of different drug interventions, dosage choices, disease typing, disease staging, gene mutations, and other factors. In conclusion, WD patients are exposed to accumulation of lipoacylated proteins and disorder of iron-sulfur cluster protein, leading to severe oxidative stress damage. Chelation therapy can alleviate the infulences of cuproptosis, thereby relieving disorders of iron-sulfur cluster protein and damages caused by oxidative stress. The cuproptosis pathway may be involved in reversing the course of WD hepatic fibrosis.
